A mental stop is a promise you make to yourself at the worst possible time. The stop goes a few cents under 48.80 and only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: No stop order, no position. The stop lives with the broker.

wrong.A phone alert at the stop price: An alert only tells you. It can't sell anything while you're in a meeting.
wrong.A mental stop you promise to keep: A stop in your head isn't a stop. It needs a real order.
wrong.Place it after the meeting: The meeting is exactly when you're unprotected. The order goes in when you buy.

questions.simple: A real stop order with the broker. It sells for you when you can't watch.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: Two days after you buy, the pop is weak and drifting toward your stop. You leave the stop right where it is.
questions.why: True. A weak start is exactly what the stop is for. Move it down to give it room and a small planned loss turns into a bigger one you never signed up for. The stop only moves up. If it hits, it hits, and you wait for the next trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A stop moves up or stays. A weak start never moves it down.
questions.simple: True. A weak start is why the stop exists, and lowering it only makes the loss bigger.

reasons: the stop rule is the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: We only buy a Wedge Pop in a stock that's above its 200-day moving average.
questions.why: True. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That line is the long-term trend, and a pop under it is mostly a bounce inside a downtrend. About half of all pops come under it, and we skip every one. The only exception is indexes and levered ETFs, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. A Wedge Pop in a stock is neither.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day or it's not our pop, however clean the base.
questions.simple: True. The 200-day is the long-term trend, and under it we don't buy stocks, however clean the base.

reasons: the 200-day rule is the owner's settled rulebook line (B26)

questions.q: Before you buy a pop, you check the index. Which picture says it's still falling and the pop can fail?
choices: One down day on big volume
questions.why: Lower lows with the averages falling. That's an index still going down. A pop against that is swimming upstream, because most stocks go where the market goes. Higher lows with rising averages is the opposite, a market turning up. One heavy down day is just one day. I want to see the index stop making new lows before I lean on pops.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index first. Still making lower lows, I wait on pops.

questions.story: A stock bottomed on Monday after a sharp decline. On Tuesday and Wednesday it closed tight under its 10 and 20-day EMAs. Thursday it gapped above both averages and above those two days' highs, and closed above both.
questions.q: Is Thursday a Wedge Pop buy by our card?
choices: No; the base ran only 2 sessions
Yes; a gap over the pivot is an A+ pop
Yes; it closed above both averages
No; a base needs at least 10 sessions
questions.answer: No; the base ran only 2 sessions
questions.why: No. The base needs at least 3 sessions after the low, with at least half the closes at or under the higher average. This one ran only 2, Tuesday and Wednesday. TraderLion: no lasting bottom until the stock tests the averages and has a few days to retreat. Without the base this is a rebound, not a Wedge Pop. Buying in the window before the base is built is a named mistake.
questions.simple: No, because the base needs at least three sessions after the low, and this one ran only two.
questions.lesson_line: Count the base. Fewer than three sessions after the low is a rebound, not a pop.

wrong.Yes; a gap over the pivot is an A+ pop: A gap through the pivot and the averages is the A+ pop, but only once the base is built. Two sessions are too few.
wrong.Yes; it closed above both averages: A close above both averages is a cross. A cross alone is not a Wedge Pop, because it needs the tight base first.
wrong.No; a base needs at least 10 sessions: The card needs at least 3 sessions after the low, not 10. A few days to retreat is enough.

questions.q: Six clean Wedge Pops sit at their pivots. How many do you buy first?
questions.story: The app's market filter has just turned Green after a market correction. Green allows full risk per grade.
choices: A few, then more as they work
All six at full size, right away
All six, at half size each
None, wait a full month first
questions.answer: A few, then more as they work
questions.why: A few first. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all six, the turn fails, and six stops hit at once. Start with a few. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add more names. If they fail, you lost a little and you're still mostly in cash. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: After a correction, start with a few positions. Add more as the first ones work.

wrong.None, wait a full month first: Green says we can trade. Waiting a month throws away the early leaders. Start small instead.
wrong.All six at full size, right away: If the turn fails, six stops hit together. Start with a few and add as they work.
wrong.All six, at half size each: Half size on all six still puts six stops in play at once. Count positions: start with a few.

questions.simple: A few. A turn can fail, so let the first ones prove it before you add more names.
